craft_claim: Audiences seek meaning as well as pleasure, so bleak works can be valued rather than merely endured; the grim tone succeeds when it converts suffering into significance, not when it merely administers pain.

supporting_evidence.note: Oliver and Raney distinguish hedonic motivations (pleasure, enjoyment) from eudaimonic motivations (meaning, insight, poignancy) in entertainment selection, providing the framework for why audiences choose difficult works.
Smuts surveys the paradox of painful art: negative responses need not reduce artistic value, and appreciation can rest on cognitive or formal rewards.

This study of empathic distress and cinematic tragedy anchors the 'sad film' line of research: tragic pleasure is investigated as arising in relation to, not simply in the absence of, empathic distress.

counterevidence.note: Section B cites Oliver and Raney for hedonic versus eudaimonic motivations in entertainment selection rather than for how a given bleak work is appraised once consumed, and section C records as contested whether unrelieved bleakness can still carry meaning or only sensation, so 'valued rather than endured' is a possibility rather than a property of the material.

scope: Film, fiction, drama, and any narrative that asks the audience to accept sustained negative affect.
exceptions: Instrumental or deliberate suffering without significance (torture-focused spectacle) may attract only curiosity or habituation, not eudaimonic value.
